howard-john-george.name: John George Howard
howard-john-george.title: Architect, Surveyor & Founder of High Park
howard-john-george.bio: Born John Corby in Hertfordshire, England, Howard emigrated to York (Toronto) in 1832 and changed his name soon after. He became the first professional architect in Upper Canada, the city's official surveyor (1843–1855), and a teacher at Upper Canada College. He laid out the Esplanade and subdivided Toronto Island, designed dozens of homes, churches and public buildings, and in 1873 donated the land that became High Park — where he and his wife Jemima are buried near the home he built, Colborne Lodge.

He and his wife Jemima lived here until his death in 1890; both are buried nearby beneath a cairn he designed himself, topped with a fence salvaged from a shipwreck that originally stood around St Paul's Cathedral in London. The house is now a museum displaying Howard's own watercolours and woodcarvings.

william-thomas.name: William Thomas
william-thomas.title: Architect, Engineer & Founding President of the Toronto Society of Arts
william-thomas.bio: Born in Suffolk, England, Thomas trained as a carpenter-joiner and builder before becoming an architect, working two decades in Leamington Spa before a building-trade depression sent him to Toronto in 1843. In under two decades he designed and supervised over 100 buildings across Ontario — including some of Toronto's most important 19th-century landmarks — and trained the next generation of architects, including William George Storm. He was a founding president of the Toronto Society of Arts (1847) and, when Howard travelled to England in 1853, served as city engineer in his place, overseeing work on the Esplanade.

frederic-cumberland.name: Frederic W. Cumberland
frederic-cumberland.title: Architect, Engineer & Railway Manager
frederic-cumberland.bio: Born in London, England, Cumberland trained as an architect through the British Admiralty's Civil Architects Department before emigrating to Toronto in 1847. In partnership first with Thomas Ridout and then with William George Storm — himself trained under William Thomas — Cumberland designed many of Toronto's most significant Victorian-era buildings. He won the competition for St James' Cathedral in open contest against ten other entrants in 1849, and later balanced his architectural career with work as chief engineer and managing director of the Northern Railway, eventually leaving architecture for railways and politics, serving in both the Ontario legislature and the House of Commons.
frederic-cumberland.source: Dictionary of Canadian Biography / Canadian Encyclopedia

henry-pellatt.name: Sir Henry Pellatt
henry-pellatt.title: Financier, Soldier & Builder of Casa Loma
henry-pellatt.bio: Born in Kingston and raised in Toronto, Pellatt joined his father's stockbroking firm as a young man and built one of early 20th-century Canada's great fortunes — by 1901 he chaired 21 companies spanning mining, insurance, real estate, and electricity, and in 1902 his consortium built the first hydroelectric generating station at Niagara Falls, earning him a reputation as 'the man who lit up Toronto.' In parallel, he rose through the ranks of the Queen's Own Rifles of Canada, which he had joined as a private at 17 and commanded from 1901; his decades of personal financial support for the regiment — including funding a 600-man trip to England for its 50th anniversary in 1910 — earned him a knighthood in 1905. Starting in 1911, with a fortune estimated at $17 million, he spent lavishly to build Casa Loma, a 98-room castle designed by architect E.J. Lennox. The First World War and the provincial expropriation of his electric power business left him deeply in debt; he and Lady Pellatt left Casa Loma in 1923, and in 1933 its remaining contents were auctioned off for a fraction of their value. He died in 1939 in a modest Mimico apartment he shared with his former chauffeur, and was given a full military funeral by the regiment he had devoted his life to.
henry-pellatt.source: Dictionary of Canadian Biography / Wikipedia / Queen's Own Rifles of Canada Regimental Museum

stops.name: Casa Loma
stops.role: His castle, designed by architect E.J. Lennox — now a museum and one of Toronto's top tourist attractions
stops.description: Pellatt had been fascinated by European castles since a teenage trip abroad, and sketched their towers and turrets from memory when planning his own. Casa Loma's 98 rooms included a great hall, a wood-panelled study, an 800-foot tunnel to the stables, and stables with mahogany stalls and each horse's name spelled out in 18-karat gold. The Pellatts moved in in 1913 but lived there only a decade before financial collapse forced them out in 1923; the city took it over for unpaid taxes a decade later.

adam-beck.name: Sir Adam Beck
adam-beck.title: Founder & Chairman of Ontario Hydro
adam-beck.bio: Born in Baden, Canada West, to a German immigrant foundryman, Beck made his early fortune manufacturing cigar boxes before entering politics as mayor of London, Ontario, and an MPP. Campaigning on the slogan 'Power at Cost' and the promise that 'the poorest working man will have electric light in his home,' he convinced Premier James Whitney to create the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario in 1906, with Beck as its first and only chairman until his death. His public utility competed directly with Toronto's private power companies — including Sir Henry Pellatt's Electrical Development Company — and in the winter of 1907–8 Toronto voters approved by-laws to buy power from Hydro instead. A 110,000-volt transmission line from Niagara Falls to Toronto opened in 1910, and in 1920 Ontario Hydro purchased the Toronto Power Plant and Toronto Electric Light Company outright, ending the 'Hydro Wars' and Pellatt's electricity business for good. Knighted in 1914, Beck died in 1925 having built what was then the largest publicly owned power utility in the world; the Sir Adam Beck generating stations at Niagara Falls carry his name today.

frederick-banting.name: Sir Frederick Banting
frederick-banting.title: Co-discoverer of Insulin, Nobel Laureate
frederick-banting.bio: Born on a farm near Alliston, Ontario, Banting trained in medicine at the University of Toronto and served as a battlefield surgeon in the First World War, earning the Military Cross. In May 1921, working in physiologist J.J.R. Macleod's lab with medical student Charles Best, he began the experiments that isolated insulin — first successfully used to treat a diabetic patient in 1922. In 1923 Banting and Macleod shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, the first ever awarded to Canadians and, at 32, the youngest recipient in the category's history. Furious that Macleod rather than Best had been honoured, Banting split his prize money with Best. He became director of the new Banting and Best Department of Medical Research that year, was knighted in 1934, and continued research on problems from cancer to aviation medicine. While serving as a wartime medical liaison officer in 1941, he was killed in a plane crash in Newfoundland at age 49.
frederick-banting.source: Nobel Prize biographical archive / Encyclopaedia Britannica / Canadian Medical Hall of Fame

lester-pearson.name: Lester B. Pearson
lester-pearson.title: 14th Prime Minister of Canada, Nobel Peace Prize Laureate
lester-pearson.bio: Born in Newtonbrook (now part of Toronto) and raised partly in East York, Pearson served in the First World War before becoming a historian, diplomat, and politician. As Canada's Secretary of State for External Affairs from 1948 to 1957, he was a key figure in founding NATO and, during the 1956 Suez Crisis, proposed creating the United Nations Emergency Force — the first large-scale UN peacekeeping mission, a model used ever since. For this he was awarded the 1957 Nobel Peace Prize. As Prime Minister from 1963 to 1968, his minority governments introduced universal medicare, the Canada Pension Plan, and in 1965 Canada's red maple leaf flag, which he had championed despite fierce opposition.

timothy-eaton.name: Timothy Eaton
timothy-eaton.title: Founder of Eaton's Department Store
timothy-eaton.bio: Born in Ballymena, Ireland, Eaton immigrated to Ontario as a young man and, after a failed bakery venture, opened a dry-goods store at 178 Yonge Street in Toronto in 1869. He built it into Canada's largest department store chain by pioneering retail practices that were radical at the time: fixed prices with no haggling, cash only, and a money-back guarantee summed up in the store's famous slogan, 'Goods Satisfactory or Money Refunded.' From 1884, his mail-order catalogue brought big-city department-store goods to rural and Western Canadian households for the first time, reshaping how Canadians shopped for generations. He died in 1907; his widow Margaret and son Sir John Craig Eaton built the Timothy Eaton Memorial Church in his honour, and the company he founded remained a dominant force in Canadian retail until its bankruptcy in 1999.

glenn-gould.name: Glenn Gould
glenn-gould.title: Pianist & Recording Artist
glenn-gould.bio: Born in Toronto on September 25, 1932, Glenn Gould became one of the most celebrated pianists of the 20th century. A child prodigy, he gave his first public concert at Eaton Auditorium in 1945 and debuted with the Toronto Symphony Orchestra at age 14. His 1955 recording of Bach's Goldberg Variations brought him worldwide recognition. He famously retired from concert performance in 1964 to focus on studio recording, pioneering a meticulous, deeply personal approach to the craft. Gould died in Toronto on October 4, 1982, just days after his 50th birthday.
glenn-gould.source: Toronto Archives / Toronto Plaques / Dictionary of Canadian Biography

stops.name: 32 Southwood Drive
stops.role: Childhood home — marked with a bronze plaque
stops.description: Glenn Gould was born and grew up in this house in The Beach neighbourhood. A bronze plaque marks the site, noting that he gave his first public concert on the organ at Eaton Auditorium on December 12, 1945, and made his debut as a soloist with the Toronto Symphony Orchestra at age 14.

stops.name: Old City Hall — Council Chambers

stops.description: In 1956, Mayor Nathan Phillips presented Glenn Gould with a watch in the Council Chambers of Old City Hall — a civic honour following the international success of his Bach Goldberg Variations recording. Three photographs of this ceremony survive in the City of Toronto Archives (Fonds 1257, Series 1057).

laura-secord.name: Laura Secord
laura-secord.title: War of 1812 Heroine
laura-secord.bio: Born Laura Ingersoll in Great Barrington, Massachusetts in 1775, Laura Secord emigrated with her family to Upper Canada in 1795 and settled in the Niagara region. In June 1813, during the American occupation of Queenston following the Battle of Queenston Heights, she overheard American officers planning a surprise attack on a British outpost at Beaver Dams. On June 23, 1813, she set out alone on foot — travelling nearly 30 kilometres through difficult terrain — to warn British commander Lieutenant James FitzGibbon. The intelligence contributed to the British and Indigenous victory at the Battle of Beaver Dams. Though largely unrecognized in her lifetime, Secord became a celebrated Canadian hero in the late 19th century. She died in Chippawa (Niagara Falls) in 1868 at the age of 93. The Laura Secord candy company, founded in Toronto in 1913, was named in her honour.
laura-secord.source: Dictionary of Canadian Biography / Toronto Public Library Archives

The City of Toronto Archives holds four photographs from the incident: two of the store exterior, a portrait of Police Constable Glover (badge 202) who responded to the scene, and a portrait of the suspect Alex Sturgeon of 541 Carlaw Avenue. The Laura Secord candy company had been founded in Toronto in 1913, named after the War of 1812 heroine.

john-craig-eaton.name: Sir John Craig Eaton
john-craig-eaton.title: Merchant, Philanthropist & Builder of Ardwold
john-craig-eaton.bio: Born in 1876, John Craig Eaton was the son of retail empire founder Timothy Eaton. After his father's death in 1907, John took over the family business and expanded it dramatically. He was known for his flamboyant philanthropy — donating ambulances, armoured cars, and hospital equipment during the First World War — and was knighted in 1915. In 1909, he built Ardwold, a 50-room mansion on Davenport Road near Casa Loma, named from the Gaelic for 'green hill.' The estate had a conservatory, swimming pool, pipe organ, fountain, and its own private hospital — in which John died of pneumonia in 1922 at just 46. Unable to find a buyer wealthy enough to maintain it, his widow Lady Flora eventually auctioned off the contents and had the mansion demolished in 1936 — its walls were so thick that dynamite was used. The land was subdivided into what is now Ardwold Gate.
john-craig-eaton.source: City of Toronto Archives / Toronto Public Library / Dictionary of Canadian Biography

stops.name: Ardwold, Davenport Road
stops.role: The 50-room mansion — demolished by dynamite
stops.address: Davenport Road at Huron Street (now Ardwold Gate), Toronto
stops.description: In 1909 Sir John Craig Eaton built Ardwold — Gaelic for 'green hill' — on Davenport Road, next door to Casa Loma. The 50-room mansion included a conservatory, swimming pool, pipe organ, fountain, and a private hospital. John's father Timothy's house in the Annex hadn't appealed to him partly because it had no garage for his Rolls-Royce. After John died of pneumonia in Ardwold's private hospital in 1922, his widow Lady Flora used the estate for some years before moving permanently to Eaton Hall Farm in King City in 1936. The contents were auctioned off and the mansion was demolished — the walls were so thick that dynamite was the easiest solution. The land was subdivided and the new streets named Ardwold Gate. Four photographs from 1922 survive, showing the mansion from multiple angles.
